<med>EPDS introduction</med>

Hello—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential and will help us figure out the best next steps for supporting you. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you today. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Hi Sarah… I guess I’m ready.

Um, laughing? Honestly, not much. I can still chuckle if something’s really funny, but it feels kind of forced. Most days I just don’t feel like laughing at all.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often… maybe once or twice I sort-of laughed, but it didn’t feel like it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get a little excited about a couple things—like when my sister said she’d bring over coffee tomorrow—but mostly I don’t really look forward to much anymore. It’s like the color’s been drained out of everything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that. If the baby’s fussy or I can’t get her to nap, I keep thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m already failing as a mom. It pops into my head even when I know, rationally, that babies just cry. I’d say that’s been happening most days this week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly imagine her choking, or I’ll lie down and picture something awful happening in her crib. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just race and I can’t shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts racing and I feel shaky even though nothing’s happening. It hits me out of nowhere, maybe every other day, and I have to sit and breathe until it passes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water. Even little stuff—dishes piling up, a text I forgot to answer—feels overwhelming, like I’m constantly one step behind and about to drown.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning with worries and “what-ifs.” I’d say four or five nights this week I was still awake an hour after I went to bed, and when I do drift off I wake up at least once or twice with my heart racing.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like a gray cloud that settles over me the moment I open my eyes. I still get up and do what I have to, but the sadness is just—there, lingering in the background all the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yeah… I cried twice this week. Once when she wouldn’t stop crying and I couldn’t figure out what she needed, and another time when I dropped a plate and it just felt like the last straw.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s… it’s crossed my mind. Just brief flashes, like “what if I wasn’t here,” but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to act on it. Still, the thought has popped up once or twice when everything feels too heavy.

You've shared that over the past week most days feel heavy and gray, with little joy or laughter, constant worry, sudden panicky waves, draining sleep, and frequent tears. While you're caring for your baby and managing the essentials, you also describe feeling overwhelmed, blaming yourself for every hiccup, and even brief flashes of wondering whether everyone might be better off if you weren't here. Your honesty highlights how hard postpartum life has become and how much support you deserve right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response indicates noticeable reduction in ability to enjoy humor, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring "most days this week" and describes pervasive guilt about her parenting, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, racing anxious thoughts without real cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sudden, unexpected panic episodes occurring every other day, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, inability to keep up, and feeling close to drowning, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, severe sleep disruption nearly every night due to racing thoughts and anxiety, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily sadness that overshadows her entire day, aligning with 'most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying twice in the past week due to feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 25 falls well above the ≥14 threshold that flags probable major depression requiring urgent evaluation. You endorsed core depressive symptoms (sadness, anhedonia, tearfulness, guilt, sleep loss) plus prominent anxiety and brief suicidal ideation without intent, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The scale's Item 10 score ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. Combined with functional impairment and maternal distress, this pattern indicates clinically significant mood disturbance needing prompt professional attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local <med>perinatal mental health team</med>
2. Ask about same-day <med>crisis counselling</med> or emergency department if self-harm thoughts intensify or plans develop
3. Bring baby to appointment or request telephone/video consult if leaving home feels impossible
4. Enlist partner/family to handle night feeds where possible so you can obtain 3-4 hour uninterrupted sleep blocks
5. Begin gentle daily movement (10-min stroller walk, stretching) and balanced snacks every 3-4 h to stabilise energy and mood
6. Limit online doom-scrolling; replace with calming audio (music, guided breathing) to reduce bedtime arousal
7. Keep brief mood log (1-10 scale) and note any escalating thoughts of harm to share with clinician
8. Identify trusted friend/family member for 15-min check-in call each evening to bolster support and safety
9. Store local 24-h crisis line number in your phone for immediate professional support if distress spikes
10. Discuss with clinician evidence-based options including <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and medication compatible with breastfeeding if indicated
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note**

**Chief concerns endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Daily excessive guilt/self-blame regarding parenting adequacy (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety (Q4) and episodic panic symptoms (Q5) without clear precipitant  
- Subjective overwhelm and difficulty coping with routine tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia: initial and middle-of-night wakening with racing thoughts (Q7)  

**Pattern summary**  
Symptoms present most days over the past week, interfere with sleep and daily functioning, and exceed typical postpartum adjustment stress.

**Safety flag**  
Passive, transient self-harm ideation reported ("what if I wasn’t here") without intent or plan (Q10).

**Screening significance**  
Findings are consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety; further clinical evaluation recommended to confirm diagnosis and assess risk.
